newsitem.title: USA: Stocks stagger in worst week ever for Dow index.
newsitem.headline: Stocks stagger in worst week ever for Dow index.

text.p: The Dow Jones industrial average posted its second-biggest point loss ever on Friday, shaken partly by an earnings warning from consumer products giant Gillette Co.
The blue-chip Dow closed down 247.37 points, or 3.1 percent, at 7,694.66, its lowest close since June.
The decline contributed to a loss for the week of 336.56 points, making it the largest weekly loss in the history of the average.
The drop was the steepest point fall since Oct. 19, 1987, the so-called Black Monday when the Dow sank 508 points, or 23 percent, to 1,738.74.
In percentage terms, Friday's decline failed to rank among the top 10.
In the broader market, declining issues swamped advances 2,116 to 714 on active volume of 534 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
Adding to the day's volatility was the "double-witching" expiration of options on stocks and stock indexes.
With the loss, the Dow has fallen 6.8 percent from its all-time closing high of 8,259.31, set on Aug. 6.
Several analysts said the downturn, the first sustained market decline since the nearly 10 percent correction that ended in mid-April, did not yet appear to be at its end.
"We are in a correction from the 8,300 level and we need to be tested a little further on the downside," said James Volk, head of institutional equity trading at Arcadia Investment Corp.
The market suffered a case of the nerves at the opening bell, with the Dow falling more than 100 points in the first few minutes of trading.

Traders were rattled after Gillette told analysts it expects disappointing 1997 earnings. On the heels of a similar warnings from Coca-Cola Co. earlier this month, that sparked considerable worry about corporate America's future profits.
Analysts believed that the market's downdraft was not the signal of the beginning of a bear market, though some said they had noticed a distinct shift in the mood on Wall Street.

"We're witnessing a transition from buy on weakness to sell on strength ... and it wouldn't surprise me if what we're seeing is the footsteps of some program trading," said Charlie Crane, chief market strategist at Key Asset Management.
He said the raging bullishness that was the hallmark of July's stock market no longer had the support of lower bond interest rates.
Analysts said the market fall was exaggerated because many traders were not at work on a summer Friday afternoon, so fewer buyers were around to step in on the weakness.
Last Friday, stocks were also clobbered with the Dow dropping 156 points.
In the bond market, the yield on the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond hovered at Thursday's close of 6.55 percent.

Consumer products stocks took it on the chin after Gillette's warning. Gillette slumped 4-5/16 to close at 85-7/8 and Procter & Gamble Co. lost 7-1/2 to 136-9/16. Colgate-Palmolive Co. fell 4-15/16 to 65-1/4.
The Nasdaq Composite index fell 24.66 points to 1,562.03.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks dropped 23.96 to 900.81. The American Stock Exchange index was off 4.88 to 635.51.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks fell 10.56 to 469.10. The average share was down 99 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was 8,631.365 down 175.921 or 2.00 percent.
